query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In chemically complex HEA nanoparticles, ultrafast femtosecond LSPR-induced heating triggers a rapid, non-equilibrium diffusion that leads to selective surface atom reordering, forming a transient, passivating layer enriched with high surface‐energy elements. This rearrangement reduces the local premelting threshold compared to the nanoparticle core, thereby governing the onset of melting and consolidating the solid solution upon rapid cooling.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, colloidally dispersed iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with a homogeneous solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Apply femtosecond laser pulses tuned to excite the LSPR of the HEA nanoparticles, providing rapid energy deposition over picosecond timescales.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in a colloidal solution to limit particle coalescence; heating energies slightly above conventional thermal activation but within the range used in noble metal nanoparticle studies; particle sizes and compositions typical for HEA systems.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a transient core–shell configuration where the nanoparticle surface becomes enriched in high surface-energy elements due to differential diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Rapid, localized heating via femtosecond LSPR excitation drives non-equilibrium atomic diffusion. Elements with lower dissolution potentials or lower surface energies migrate away from the surface, while elements with inherently higher surface energies accumulate to form a passivating shell. This surface reordering modulates the local melting behavior by lowering the energy barrier for premelting at the surface while preserving the interior’s solid solution, thereby assisting in the subsequent consolidation during rapid cooling.
generation.predicted_outcome: When subjected to femtosecond LSPR-induced heating, HEA nanoparticles will exhibit early-stage, surface-localized premelting (manifested as a thin liquid-like shell) and a measurable compositional gradient with enrichment of high surface-energy elements at the surface. This behavior will contrast with conventionally heated nanoparticles, which will display more uniform melting and coalescence.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles heated using conventional (slower) thermal annealing methods without femtosecond LSPR excitation, expected to show uniform melting behavior and greater tendency for coalescence.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to colloidal HEA nanoparticles within the size and composition ranges typical of iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper systems, under rapid heating conditions that do not allow extensive atomic diffusion beyond the transient surface reordering. It may not hold under extreme thermal regimes or for significantly different alloy systems.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative shifts in melting thresholds and the extent of surface enrichment are currently uncertain and require systematic experimental calibration. The relative roles of each elemental species in forming the passivating layer also remain to be fully elucidated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of colloidal iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles. Subject one set to femtosecond LSPR-induced heating while using conventional thermal annealing on the other set as a control. Use in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to monitor real-time structural and compositional changes during heating and subsequent cooling.
measurements: In situ TEM imaging to detect the onset and progression of premelting and possible core–shell formation.
EDS elemental mapping to quantify surface versus core composition before, during, and after heating.
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine shifts in premelting or melting temperatures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If femtosecond LSPR-induced heating does not produce a measurable surface enrichment of high surface-energy elements or if the HEA nanoparticles exhibit a homogeneous melting behavior similar to the conventional heating control (i.e., no significant difference in melting thresholds or structural reordering is observed), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Unfortunately, heat-assisted synthesis of alloy nanoparticles is less successful than in bulk because melting and sintering processes tend to favor their coalescence into larger particles and their reshaping into spheres (i.e., loss of dimensional, morphological, and aggregation state control), demanding the use of suitable substrates to prevent such issues. In this scenario, an ideal method of alloy nanoparticle synthesis would be to provide control over size, shape, and composition of colloidal synthesis routes with that delivered by high-temperature routes to obtain alloys. The SAED patterns are in agreement with the XRD results, revealing that the crystal structure of CrMnFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles is FCC solid solution. By analyzing the TEM images and EDS elemental mappings (Fig. 1h), all five elements relatively homogeneously are distributed within the CrMnFeCoNi HEA nanoparticles, in which the contents of the Fe, Co and Ni elements are higher than those of the Cr and Mn (Fig. S3), benefiting from their closer reduction potential and fewer valence electrons that form stable compounds while Mn is expected to be partially vaporized during the laser synthesis due to its higher vapor pressure. Moreover, the boiling temperature of 2334 K (Table S3) of Mn is the lowest and close to the highest temperature induced by laser, thus the Mn element has a relatively high possibility to evaporate. The HRTEM images in Fig. 1f and Fig. S4b–d, also show that the HEA nanoparticles are partially embraced by several graphene layers. This is similar to carbon-shell-encapsulated nanoparticles that were reported and achieved by Sharma et al. for improved catalytic durability on electrochemical reactions,.

Besides supporting intuitive results, such as elements with low reduction potential depleting from the surface through dissolution, our demonstrations show that a model built on this framework gains insight into less intuitive outcomes, notably, how interactions between elements impact the degree to which a particle with a given composition dissolves and changes surface composition. Moreover, trends in the literature showing core–shell formation were reproducible despite the simplicity of the dissolution model used to demonstrate the presented framework. Further validation could entail experimentally verifying that elements with high surface energy in sub-surface layers can stabilize atoms on the surface. Utilizing the current model for other predictions than investigating trends is likely to have little validity. However, further development toward a more rigorous dissolution model within this framework could increase prediction accuracy. reading.lever: Apply femtosecond LSPR-induced heating to colloidal HEA nanoparticles to rapidly access premelting regimes while limiting coalescence.
reading.why: This approach, proven in noble metal systems, directly enables controlled thermal processing to study rapid premelting and solid solution consolidation in chemically complex nanoparticles.
